responseSet.title: Anorexia Nervosa as a Stage of Recovery in the Treatment of an Adolescent Girl
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Anorexia Nervosa as a Stage of Recovery in the Treatment of an Adolescent Girl

Robina Prestage

Robina Prestage

Robina Prestage  

It is my intention in this account to attempt to bring together the essence of a talk given by the late Dr. John Bolland and myself at the Centre for the Study of Adolescence in February, 1973. I am indebted to Dr. M. Glasser of the Brent Consultation Centre for the excellent minutes of the meeting, which now serve to amplify the notes that we had extracted from a voluminous file that accumulated over the 5 year period of treatment.

In discussing our presentation of this case, Dr. Bolland and I realised that in selecting the pseudonym “Ruth” for this fifteen-year-old patient, we were unconsciously referring to certain associations — for instance, during the anorexia phase the girl was indeed “ruthless” in the sense that Winnicott employs it, and Ruth's mother certainly identified with the biblical character of that name, in that I became her “Naomi” in the transference. “Ruth clave unto her” and said “Entreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go … where thou diest, will I die”.

The initial referral came as an urgent request from the G.P. and as it was presented as an emergency situation Dr. Bolland and I arranged to see mother and daughter the following day. Ruth was booked to fly to Australia to spend Easter with her father who had been divorced from her mother since Ruth was eight years old. She was said to be severely depressed and it was thought she might be suicidal. However, after her consultation with Dr. Bolland he decided he should trust her to make the trip and made an appointment to see her again on the day of her return.

From that meeting there followed an incessant outpouring of her writings that was to continue unabated for the next three years. Dr. Bolland felt that these efforts, some of which will be quoted, were eloquent and poignant expressions of her condition.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Brief Work with Adolescents and Young Adults in a Counselling Service

Beta Copley

Beta Copley

Beta Copley  

The work I am about to describe is in the framework of a service which undertakes brief interventions with young people based on psychoanalytical knowledge. It was originally set up in the belief that certain adolescents in difficulty could be helped by an attempt at understanding which would be brief in nature and offered quickly. It was thought that such an intervention would be both helped by, and in its turn could help, normal growth and development. A number of young people of course would obviously require something more.

I propose in this paper to refer mainly to clinical material and problems, but will first say something about the setting in which I work, which is that of the Young People's Counselling Service at the Tavistock Clinic, London. The service is administratively linked to the Adolescent Department, but is clinically independent. It is staffed by child psychotherapists, clinical psychologists and social workers, all of whom are also engaged in longer term work. It has no direct access to the treatment services provided by other departments. I am grateful to my colleagues for helpful clinical discussions, but can of course only speak for my own work. We offer a series of appointments, normally up to four, with the possibility of a review, if wished, after a few months. Our clients are usually self-referred young people, although we do occasionally see parents or young couples. We do not have a rigid age limit. It is not a dropin service but appointments are usually offered within a few days time. The client comes to us directly without any intermediary apart from a telephone call or visit to our Secretary, who may be able to filter out a few people who would obviously be better referred elsewhere. Some workers like their clients to write something about themselves and their reasons for coming before they are seen. I prefer myself to experience the unknown situation with the client directly in the first instance, as I think this facilitates work in the counter transference, of which I will say more later.

[[RunningHead]]

Lucy, 21 months, in foster care for 19 days by Joyce and James Robertson (Film series and guide-book, Young Children in Brief Separation obtainable from Concord Films Council, Nacton, Ipswich, Suffolk, U.K.).

Gianna Henry

Gianna Henry

Gianna Henry  

Lucy is the last film of the series Young children in brief separation. Except for John, who was for nine days in a residential nursery, the other four children were all fostered at the Robertson's home while their mother was having a second baby. The aim of this research was to explore how the stress of an early separation might be modified and the risks to development minimised by the responsive attention of a single mother substitute, as opposed to multiple caretaking.

Lucy gives us an opportunity for reflecting on issues that were less prominent in Jane, Kate and Thomas. It highlights in particular some of the problems inherent in the beginning and ending of a fostering relationship.

When Mrs. Robertson visits Lucy in her home, before the mother's confinement, we see a very cautious little girl who never smiles. Her mother also comes across as lacking in vitality and rather cut off. She is described as being in a rather subdued mood in the latter stages of her pregnancy.

Lucy brings her cautiousness with her when she first goes to the Robertsons’. She whimpers a little in her sleep during the first night in their house, but otherwise she does not make herself much heard. Her vocabulary is restricted to two words: “Thank you” and “Quackers”. “Quackers” is a hard rubber duck, her favourite toy. She has no soft labial sound for mummy. This seems significant in a twenty-one-month-old who can already manage the difficult “Quackers”.

It sems to me that Lucy started her very good experience with the Robertsons, relying on poorer internal resources than those which John, four months younger than she, had when he first entered the residential nursery. He seemed to keep the hope going and persisted in the attempt to establish a close relationship with one of the nurses. It took a while for him to give up. His initial capacity for trust and his expectation to find containment were much greater than Lucy's.

Lucy does not reach out very much at first, she even struck me at times as a little withdrawn, but gradually, during the first week, she begins to come to life, as if something were revived in her. Her appearance changes. After a week she is described as “lively, good humoured and more affectionate”. The sparkle has come back.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Atmosphere in the Labour Ward

Emanuel Lewis

Emanuel Lewis

Emanuel Lewis  

Frederick Leboyer, in his film and in his book Birth without Violence (Leboyer, 1975) has drawn our attention to the feelings and the needs of the newborn baby. Through his work we are made poignantly aware of the trauma of birth, and of the baby's anxiety at the primary separation from mother. The film, by focusing our attention in detail, in close-up, on the baby makes us deeply aware of the infant's feelings, needs and capacities. Yet the film also distances us from the anxiety arousing events, thereby freeing our capacity to observe. That the film is in black and white further distances us from the bloody anxiety of birth in colour.

In the labour ward the conscious and unconscious awareness of the infant's anxieties at the birth, gives rise to anxiety in the adults attending the labour. This is counter-transference anxiety, which in obstetric staff may lead to the mismanagement of labour. For example, in Birth without Violence Leboyer gives as his opinion that the unconscious reawakening of the adult's memory of pain of his own birth and the need to deny and forget this pain, is a reason for our blindness to the new infant's pain. And that as a result of our blindness we are unkind to the newborn baby.

At a birth we are made particularly aware of our primitive feelings; feelings that are related to the memory of our experiences as babies. Our feelings are associated with fantasies, and these conscious and unconscious fantasies, arising as they do from our earliest experiences, are based on the body and its products. At a childbirth we are concerned with breath and breathing, with shit and blood and sweat and liquor, with milk and vomit. Dr. Leboyer's film makes us aware through close-up of the baby's sensations. We see skin and are aware of touch; we see the mouth and are made aware of breathing and sucking; we see the infant's eyes and are made aware of apparent curiosity and need to relate. Leboyer discusses in detail how the baby feels anxiety at the primary separation from his mother. The importance of separation anxiety in young children has been stressed by Dr. John Bowlby who believes that separation anxiety may be more important in human development than the anxiety associated with the Oedipus complex; and in this respect it is of interest that the story of the life of Oedipus begins with his separation at birth from both his parents.

responseSet.title: Some Effects of the Absence of His Father on an Eight Year Old Boy
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Some Effects of the Absence of His Father on an Eight Year Old Boy

Eileen Orford

Eileen Orford

Eileen Orford  

It is not easy to find papers concerned with the effect of the absent father on the early life of the child. There have been a number of papers about the effect of the father's death upon the child, for example, C.R. Reeves (1973), W. Halton (1973), and M. Harris (1973) and Meiss (1952). These papers however have been very much concerned with the effects of the death on the growing child, and the absence of the father has been overshadowed by the trauma of his death. As an increasing number of children are reared in one-parent families, the father usually being the missing parent, it becomes important to try to define the possible consequences of this family constellation, and perhaps in the process to add to our understanding of the father's part in the child's emotional growth.

Frequently referrals of such children include a suggestion that a male therapist be found. While such a suggestion is understandable, it is often difficult to implement, and, in any event, carries an implication that in some sense the therapist could, in fact, take the father's place. Referral to a woman may have advantages in that child and therapist have to work towards the development of some feeling of an internal father within the child, without as it were, external props, which the child may lack in his external situation. Andre Green (1975) notes an aspect of fathering in the complex representation of men as husbands and fathers that the mother of the baby has in her internal world to sustain her through the stresses of her relationship with the baby. In the therapeutic situation with the fatherless child, what the child has to work with is this complex representation within the therapist/mother. The child will transfer to the therapeutic situation, as Melanie Klein (1952A/B) has emphasised, those “early experiences, object relations and emotions which come to focus on the psychoanalyst: this implies that the patient deals with the conflicts and anxieties which have been reactivated by making use of mechanisms and defences as in earlier situations. The therapist can thus observe the child's infantile fantasies in his transferences to her as father, or mother or parts of each. Modification occurs by interpretation and understanding.” The male therapist must use his understanding and experience of a good breast in conveying a maternal function to patients. The woman therapist must draw on equivalent experience and understanding of a strong, benevolent father in working with the fatherless child.

[[RunningHead]]

A Child Psychotherapist in a Nurse-Patient Group

Kerry Novick

Kerry Novick

Kerry Novick  

This report is an attempt to describe a year's work in a weekly group for adolescent inpatients and their outpatient parents. The group, originally staffed by the two or three nurses on the adolescent unit, was part of the treatment offered in the small adolescent unit, which is part of the Cassel Hospital. The unit consists of about twelve adolescent inpatients, aged approximately 14-19, two to three psychiatric staff, two to three nurses, child psychotherapist, psychiatric social worker, educational psychologist, with the backup of other medical and psychotherapy staff in the hospital. The adolescent patients’ treatment included twice-weekly individual psychotherapy, twice-weekly clinical groups with their own nurse, daily area meetings of the adolescent group with its own staff and the single adult patients and staff, thrice-weekly community meetings, involving the whole hospital population, and the Parents' group. In addition to this, all patients were expected to contribute to the domestic and administrative work of the hospital, and most either studied or worked as soon as they were able.

Parents, on the other hand, had originally little formal involvement with their children's treatment programme, beyond the stage of initial consultation before admission, and the nurse's home visit. After admission of the adolescent patient, contact with the family was maintained by nurses, on the basis of mutual demand, and thus varied greatly from one family to another. A similar pattern of occasional consultation by parents with the consultant in charge of the unit prevailed. The weekly parent-adolescent group, held in the evening by the nursing staff, was at first the only formal help offered to parents, and, at the time I joined the adolescent unit, the “Parents' group” appeared to be suffering the effects of mixed feelings both in the staff and in the parents. From the side of the hospital, it seemed that we were unsure of what we wanted the group to accomplish, and, perhaps as a result of this, Parents' attendance at the group was not presented to the family as an integral and required part of the adolescents’ treatment.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

A Psychological Interpretation by J.H. Kahn, M.D., F.R.C.Psych, D.P.U. Published by Pergamon Int. Library £6.00

Frances Tustin

Frances Tustin

Frances Tustin  

This is a book that I can warmly recommend to all those who want to deepen their personal experience. Like the Book of Job, Dr. Kahn's book does not only inform and interpret but also facilitates the growth of new thoughts in the reader's mind.

The author has been growing with the book for the past twenty-five years and at the end of the Introduction he writes:-

“The most difficult task was to bring the book to a conclusion. Even after depositing the manuscript with the publishers, new ideas came to notice and new comparisons came to mind. My hope is that readers will be able to take over some of the pleasure of the discovery of new growing points.”

This has certainly been so in my own case. The new ideas it has stirred press to be formulated and written down. But a reviewer does both the author of a book, and the readers of a review, a disservice if he merely uses the review of a book as an opportunity to expound his own ideas. So let me tell you what the book is about without interposing my own thoughts too much and without spoiling your prospects of a good “read”, for this book is eminently readable and thought-provoking without being sententious and “heavy”.

The book begins with the Book of Job presented in full. Dr. Kahn then proceeds to discuss the way in which the perfectionist Job, (“a man of blameless and upright life”), has to go through the spiritual crisis which is inevitable if a compulsive and obsessional character is to free himself from his too rigid conformity to established tradition and his stereotyped, legalistic and mechanical responses. The writing is completely free from technical jargon and there is no patronising “looking down” on Job as a psychiatric case. Rather one feels that Dr. Kahn is using Job's experience to work through his own deep personal “mid-life” crisis, as indeed, William Blake seemed to use the story of Job, by representing the stages through which he passed, in a series of drawings. Kahn uses these fascinating drawings at appropriate stages throughout his book. It is a mature book written by a maturing person. He writes of how he and his secretary, Mrs. Solomon, “struggled together along with Job's struggle, sometimes arriving at an impasse in which it was possible to savour Job's depression. Eventually we came to feel that we had entered the skin of Job and endured the turmoil of the tempest.

[[RunningHead]]

Termination of Treatment of an Adolescent Boy11

Jack Novick PHD

Jack Novick

London

Jack Novick  

In the literature on the analytic treatment of adolescents there is an understandable emphasis on the technique of getting them into analysis (Aichorn, 1925; Eissler, 1958; Harley, 1970; Spiegel, 1951) and of keeping them there once they are in (Geleerd, 1957; Laufer, 1974), but as yet there is no discussion of termination or the terminal phase. Scattered in the literature are a number of brief remarks which imply that the kind of analytic termination described and discussed in regard to adults is an infrequent occurrence in the analysis of adolescents. Anna Freud (1970) points out that the adolescent revolt is often transferred to the analyst, in fact experienced for the first time with the analyst, and instead of severing the infantile tie with the parents the adolescent ends his analysis. At a scientific meeting of the Association for Child Psycho-Analysis, the members of one Workshop are reported to have noted that the analysis of adolescents often finds a “natural end” because the patient makes some external move such as leaving the city, going to university, etc. (Landauer, 1970). Even those adolescents who do not break-off treatment but reach what may be called a terminal phase often do not show any of the features said to appear regularly in the terminal phase of adult analysis. Annie Reich reports that many adolescents show a great readiness to give-up the analyst at the point of termination. She states, “In all these cases a full-blown transference had never developed. Certain secrets were never revealed. The analysis as such had been incomplete.” (1950, p. 181). Some authors (Katan, 1937; Spiegel, 1951; Adatto, 1958, 1974), see this readiness to give up the analyst as not only a frequent occurrence but a desirable one. According to Spiegel (1951) the readiness and ease of termination is a counterpart of “newly developing object-relations”. Adatto (1958, 1974) presents a series of cases in which a period of productive analytic work is followed by a marked diminution in the analysability of the transference and by massive resistance to further treatment. The cases he presented had no terminal phase and in the light of the marked improvement reported in all his patients there is the implication that a terminal phase is not only infrequent but unncessary for the achievement of treatment goals. Further Adatto in agreement with Spiegel suggests that continued treatment would have been fruitless and possibly harmful.

[[RunningHead]]

Explorations In Autism: A Psycho-Analytical Study by Donald Meltzer, John Bremner, Shirley Hoxter, Doreen Wedell and Isca WittenbergThe Roland Harris Educational Trust1975, Clunie Press, Ballechin House, Strathray, Perthshire, Scotland.

Anne Alvarez

Anne Alvarez

Anne Alvarez  

The authors of this extraordinarily beautiful book have set out to explore, describe and conceptualise certain features which they take to be discernible in the complex and well-nigh incomprehensible illness of autism. They have recorded in great detail in four psycho-analytical case studies their observations, their counter-transference, their bewilderment, and their gradual attempts to formulate and reformulate the mysterious phenomena of the mental life of these absorbing children. Confusion, lapses in transference, randomness, and in particular, meaninglessness of behaviour are only some of the problems they approached by the psycho-analytical method, which almost by definition involves an assumption of and search for meaning. Yet through an examination of the minutest details of the behaviour of these children, of sequences and repetitions, of emotion in the transference, and surprisingly, of interruptions in the transference, they have managed to locate and elucidate certain clearly defined phenomena, above all, the meaninglessness itself.

They have gone equipped with the theories of Melanie Klein and W.R. Bion, but appear to have enlarged these theories where the facts did not fit them. They do not make therapeutic claims, although all four children seem to have improved to a marked degree under the treatment. Nor do they claim to have made etiological discoveries, although some hypotheses are advanced as to possible predisposing personality factors and as to possible environmental failure of a particular kind at the period of maximum dependence in the first month of life.

These are rather by the way, however. The book is much more concerned with exploring the mental life of autistic children, and it does this with rich and illuminating precision. The main thesis of the early theoretical chapters, written by the editor, D. Meltzer, is that a particular state of mind which he terms the Autistic State Proper, can be differentiated from other types of mental functioning in these children. The latter types may consist of residues of the autism, or of certain personality tendencies which may predispose the child to autism, but are not to be equated with the autistic state itself.

[[RunningHead]]

Infantile Elements and Adult Strivings in Adolescent Sexuality11

Martha Harris

Martha Harris

Martha Harris  

When I came to write this paper I soon came to realise that its focus would have to be a much narrower one than the title allows. I also found that I was returning over and over again to analytic material from a fairly wide range of gifted adolescents who, as the world goes, were more than usually fortunate in their external circumstances, young people who from any external point of view might seem to have everything in their favour but who nevertheless seemed quite unable to enjoy their good fortune.

In all of them there existed a deep sense of unworthiness together with the quite opposite conviction of being special. There was evidence to suggest that they were regarded by one or both of their parents as special, and that they expected this treatment from the rest of the world although when it was forthcoming they could not use it to assuage their discontent. One could think of them as young people who were in the painful position of having to learn that their appearance, intelligence, emotional endowment, and social position were not evidence of innate superiority but gifts which had to be earned by carrying them and treating them as a responsibility. Difficulty in learning this showed itself clearly in their sexual attitudes and behaviour.

Defensive structures that had served them well in latency and had allowed them to have a successful and fairly untroubled development at that time, made them particularly vulnerable to the intense sexual drives and frustrations of adolescence. They tended to have difficulty in being one of the adolescent group and in using it to share experiences with peers, thereby working their way towards more adult relationships; they were impatient to leap right into the world of the grown-ups and to that “happy ever after” which is the young child's idea of marriage.

Theoretical Background

It is not possible or useful to try to present anything like a comprehensive summary of the many publications about adolescent sexuality. I shall confine myself to brief references to those which have helped me in my thinking about these cases and in particular to the two to whom I shall then refer.

Freud's Concept of Projection11

Anne Hurry , Jack Novick and Kerry Novick

Kerry Novick

Kerry Novick  

Historical Summary

Projection was first discussed by Freud in the 1890′s; at this stage projection was first of all a normal process, which could be “used” or “abused” for purposes of defence. He described the “normal” process as basic to many different phenomena, including myth, religion and primitive thinking; the various defensive uses of projection also covered a variety of processes, among which we may differentiate reflexive drive projection and externalisation of aspects of the self. These lines of thought were progressively expanded, culminating in two major papers. Totem and Taboo (1912-1913) contained Freud's major thinking on the role of projection in animism and primitive thinking in the savage or the child. Notes on a Case of Paranoia (1911c) contained his major thinking on projection as a defence.

For some years after this his main interest in this topic lay in the role of projection in the early development of the self. The particular process involved appears to contain elements of both non-defensive and defensive processes, but in Freud's later writings it is the relation of this process to the differentiation of self and object that is stressed, and by 1920 he no longer termed the process “projection” but described it as the “origin” of projection. (1920g)

Thereafter Freud continued his interest in projection until the end of his writings, gradually writing less about its non-defensive aspects, and focusing upon its defensive aspects, particularly upon the reflexive projection of the drive impulse.

It is important to note that Freud also at times used projection in a purely mechanistic or descriptive sense. Projection is a pre-analytic term, the literal meaning being “to throw in front of”: hence its usage in relation to the process by which an image is thrown on a screen. Freud's usage of the term in this metaphorical sense can be seen, for instance, in his paper on Screen Memories (1899a).

Obituary

Miss Traill MA

Miss Traill

Miss Traill  

It is with deep regret that we record the death, on December 20, 1975, of Miss P.M. Traill, after a short illness.

Born in Glasgow and educated at Roedean and at Cambridge, she was among the first group of students to have been trained in Child Psychotherapy by the late Dr. Margaret Lowenfeld.

After obtaining the Diploma of the Institute of Child Psychology she worked as a therapist first in Birmingham and later at Bramling House School, Chesterfield.

She joined the staff of the I.C.P. in 1948 when it re-opened in London after war-time evacuation. In addition to her work as a child psychotherapist, she took an active part in the Training Course from the time it was reestablished in 1949 until a few months before her death. Every student who trained at the I.C.P. after the war has good reason to remember with affection and gratitude her skilled teaching, her steady support and guidance and her total reliability.

She was a founder member of the Association of Child Psychotherapists and an office-bearer in a variety of capacities from its inception. But she was essentially a very private person who shunned the limelight and preferred to remain in the background, getting on with the job in hand.

Those of us who knew her well knew also the steadfastness of her friendship and of her many quiet acts of unobtrusive generosity.

Her true memorial, however, is the many hundreds of children she helped towards greater health, happiness and maturity during her 40 years as a child psychotherapist.
